questions.q: List all the supporting characters/elements explicitly present in the poem "मकक" as described in the NCERT text.
questions.a: The supporting characters are: the tree (हकसज), the bird (जकक), the bird's nest, the children (कपकसक), the plaster (लसव), and the wall (पकड). A wrong answer that omits the plaster or wall reveals the student treats only living beings as characters, missing the poem's personification of inanimate parts. A wrong answer that includes the mud house itself confuses protagonist with supporting cast.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the tree (हकसज) functions as a supporting character in relation to the mud house.
questions.a: The tree provides shade (उहक) and stands as an enduring, living presence beside the decaying house. It acts as a silent guardian and a foil: where the house is crumbling, the tree remains sturdy; where the house is human-made, the tree is natural. This contrast highlights the house's vulnerability and the poem's theme of nature outlasting human effort. A wrong answer that only describes the tree's physical appearance ("it is big and green") without linking it to the house shows the student cannot move from description to literary function.

questions.q: Using specific imagery from the poem, show how the bird's nest (जकक का घोंसला) reflects the theme of fragility that also surrounds the mud house.
questions.a: Step 1: Locate the line "जकक से यहिक गकवक पकडक" (the bird's nest, tired from the branch). Step 2: Note the adjectives—"यहिक" (tired), "गकवक" (weary)—that transfer human exhaustion to the nest. Step 3: Connect to the mud house: the house is also "old," its plaster eroding ("लसव की दकफेक पर पकड से जकस एयर्स"). Step 4: Conclude that both shelters—one natural, one human—are portrayed as exhausted, temporary structures at the mercy of time. A wrong answer that describes the nest as merely "a bird's home" misses the transferred epithet and the thematic parallel.

questions.q: Compare the roles of the children (कपकसक) and the plaster (लसव) as supporting characters. How do they represent opposing forces in the poem?
questions.a: The children ("वनक़र कपकसक के उगस कफक") symbolize vitality, play, and the future—they are "nests of innocent children," suggesting growth and continuity. The plaster ("लसव की दकफेक") represents erosion, exposure, and the past—it is a cliff-like edge crumbling away. Together they frame the mud house between life and decay. A wrong answer that says "both are part of the setting" fails to see them as active symbolic forces pulling the poem's emotional tone in opposite directions.

questions.q: Which single supporting character most powerfully reinforces the poem's central idea? Justify your choice with two pieces of textual evidence.
questions.a: The tree (हकसज) is the most powerful supporting character. Evidence 1: "हकसज का उहक" (the tree's shade) positions it as a protective canopy over the house, making the house's exposure more poignant. Evidence 2: The tree is described as alive and enduring ("वहकक जकक से यहिक गकवक पकडक" implies the tree/branch persists), while the house decays. This longevity makes the tree a witness to transience, embodying the poem's meditation on what lasts. A wrong answer that picks the children because "they are cute" or the plaster because "it is mentioned often" reveals an inability to weigh thematic significance against mere presence.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza from the perspective of the wall (पकड) addressing the mud house, using the poem's imagery and tone.
questions.a: A strong stanza would adopt the wall's voice: weary, observant, accepting. Example: "मैं पकड हूँ, तेरी खाल, लसव झरता है रोज़ / जकस तेरे सीने पर, कफक खेलते हैं निर्भय / हकसज का साया भी अब कम पड़ता है / हम दोनों धीरे-धीरे मिट्टी में मिलते हैं।" A poor answer would write a generic description of a wall without using the poem's specific images (plaster, children, tree) or without maintaining the melancholic, accepting tone.
